lessons.title: How a Request Travels
lessons.summary: Follow a page load from the browser to the server and back.

sections.visualNote: The first visit starts with an empty browser cache and no open connection.
sections.title: Start with a page load
sections.body:
You open a book page in an online store. The browser needs to:

1. Find the server.
2. Open a connection.
3. Request the page.

> **Assumption.** The browser has no cached DNS answer or open connection.
sections.bodyHtml:

  3. Request the page.

sections.note: The time to live (TTL) tells a cache how long it can reuse a DNS answer.
sections.visualNote: The DNS reply gives the browser an address. The resolver can answer from its own cache.
sections.title: Find the address
sections.body:
The browser needs an **IP address** for the store's domain.

1. Check the browser's cache.
2. If there is no valid answer, ask a **DNS resolver**.
3. The resolver checks its cache or queries other DNS servers.

sections.note: A round trip includes the time for a message to reach the server and for a reply to return.
sections.visualNote: This example uses TCP and TLS. Connection setup comes before the HTTP request.
sections.title: Open a secure connection
sections.body:
The browser opens a **TCP connection**. It then starts a **TLS handshake**.

During the handshake, the browser checks the server certificate. Both sides establish encryption keys.

> **Note.** Setup takes time before the first HTTP request. The browser can often reuse the connection.

lessons.title: Latency & Throughput
lessons.summary: Use latency, throughput, and concurrency to find and relieve bottlenecks.

sections.visualNote: Latency spans the time from request start until the client receives the response.
sections.title: Measure a request
sections.body:
**Latency** is the elapsed time for one operation. Assume these steps run in order:

| Work | Time |
| --- | --- |
| Network travel | 20 ms |
| Service processing | 30 ms |
| Database call | 70 ms |
| **Total** | **120 ms** |

> **Note.** When branches run in parallel, add the longest branch to the work they share.
sections.bodyHtml:
Latency is the elapsed time for one operation. Assume these steps run in order:

Work Time
Network travel 20 ms
Service processing 30 ms
Database call 70 ms
Total 120 ms

Note. When branches run in parallel, add the longest branch to the work they share.

sections.visualNote: Throughput counts completed operations in a time interval.
sections.title: Count completed work
sections.body:
**Throughput** is completed work per unit of time.

**6,000 completions ÷ 60 seconds = 100 requests/s.**

Requests can run at the same time even when each takes a long time. Count failures separately. When the queue grows, arrivals outpace completions.
sections.bodyHtml:

sections.visualNote: The percentile describes a distribution, not the duration of every request.
sections.title: Read the tail
sections.body:
A **p95 of 120 ms** means roughly 95% of requests finished within 120 ms. The result depends on the percentile method. The slowest requests can take much longer.

Record the workload and time window. Report **p99** and errors as well as the mean.

> **Warning.** Combine samples or histogram buckets across instances. Averaging each instance's percentile generally gives the wrong result.

sections.visualNote: Requests overlap while the system processes them.
sections.title: Relate latency and concurrency
sections.body:
In a stable system:

**Average requests in flight = throughput × average latency.**

At **100 completions/s** and **0.12 s** average latency, about **12 requests** are in flight.

> **Note.** Use the same system boundary and time units. This average does not predict the worst burst.

sections.visualNote: Work waits in the queue when the database completes requests more slowly than they arrive.
sections.title: Find the queue
sections.body:
The system receives **120 requests/s**. The database finishes **100/s**.

If all requests stay in the queue, the backlog grows by **20 requests/s**. That is **1,200** more requests after one minute.

Measure queue depth and wait time. Longer timeouts do not increase database capacity.

sections.visualNote: With the assumed hit rate, half of the requests avoid a database read.
sections.title: Change the bottleneck
sections.body:
Assume a cache serves **50% of 120 reads/s**. Only **60 reads/s** reach the database. Its assumed capacity is **100/s**.

Measure p95, p99, cache hit rate, and database saturation after the change.

> **Warning.** A cold cache or a burst of misses can overload the database. If writes are the bottleneck, a read cache may help little.

sections.visualNote: Measure each component and the end-to-end path to locate waiting and saturation.
sections.title: Recap: interpret the numbers
sections.body:
| Measure | Example and use |
| --- | --- |
| Latency | **120 ms** for one request. Find where it spends time. |
| Throughput | **6,000/min = 100/s**. Count completed requests. |
| Concurrency | **100/s × 0.12 s = 12** in flight on average. |
| Backlog | **120/s − 100/s = 20/s** more queued. |
| Cache | **120/s × 50% misses = 60/s** store reads. |

> **Check.** State the workload and time window. Test under realistic load and check the tail, even if average latency improves.

lessons.title: Napkin Math
lessons.summary: Turn explicit workload assumptions into traffic, bandwidth, and storage estimates.

sections.visualNote: Users produce requests; the service must handle both normal and peak traffic.
sections.title: Define the example
sections.body:
Assume a photo service has **1 million daily active users**. Each person:

- Views **20 photos** per day
- Uploads **one photo** per day

> **Units.** This example uses decimal sizes. **1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes**. **1 TB = 1,000 GB**.
sections.bodyHtml:
Assume a photo service has 1 million daily active users. Each person:

  • Views 20 photos per day
  • Uploads one photo per day

Units. This example uses decimal sizes. 1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes. 1 TB = 1,000 GB.

sections.visualNote: Divide daily requests by the number of seconds in a day.
sections.title: Convert daily traffic to a rate
sections.body:
There are **86,400 seconds** in a day.

| Operation | Average rate |
| --- | --- |
| Read | 20 million/day ÷ 86,400 ≈ **231/s** |
| Upload | 1 million/day ÷ 86,400 ≈ **11.6/s** |

Keep these rates separate. Reads and uploads can use different resources.
sections.bodyHtml:
There are 86,400 seconds in a day.

Operation Average rate
Read 20 million/day ÷ 86,400 ≈ 231/s
Upload 1 million/day ÷ 86,400 ≈ 11.6/s

Keep these rates separate. Reads and uploads can use different resources.

sections.visualNote: A peak multiplier raises the capacity target above the daily average.
sections.title: Allow for peak load
sections.body:
Assume peak traffic is **3×** the daily average.

- **Reads:** 231.5 × 3 ≈ **694/s**
- **Uploads:** 11.6 × 3 ≈ **35/s**

> **Assumption.** Events, regions, and retries can change the peak. Use measured traffic when available.
sections.bodyHtml:
Assume peak traffic is 3× the daily average.

  • Reads: 231.5 × 3 ≈ 694/s
  • Uploads: 11.6 × 3 ≈ 35/s

Assumption. Events, regions, and retries can change the peak. Use measured traffic when available.

sections.visualNote: Upload bytes cross the network before the service stores them.
sections.title: Calculate ingress bandwidth
sections.body:
At **2 MB per upload**:

- **Average:** 11.6 uploads/s × 2 MB ≈ **23 MB/s**, or **185 Mb/s**.
- **3× peak:** About **69 MB/s**, before protocol overhead.

> **Warning.** Capital **B** means bytes. Lowercase **b** means bits. One byte has **8 bits**.

sections.visualNote: The logical image is stored and replicated; copies increase physical capacity.
sections.title: Calculate storage and replication
sections.body:
Each day brings **1 million uploads × 2 MB = 2 TB** of logical data.

| Copies | Capacity for 365 days |
| --- | --- |
| One | **730 TB** |
| Three | **2,190 TB**, or **2.19 PB** |

This estimate excludes backups, indexes, other image sizes, and storage overhead. Count backups separately from replicas.

sections.visualNote: The cache serves hits; misses still read from origin storage.
sections.title: Estimate outgoing traffic and caching
sections.body:
Clients read **20 million photos/day × 2 MB = 40 TB/day**.

If caches serve **90% of the bytes**, the origin serves **4 TB/day**.

> **Note.** The byte hit rate can differ from the request hit rate. A few large misses can account for most of the bytes.

sections.visualNote: The load balancer distributes requests among service replicas.
sections.title: Test a capacity choice
sections.body:
Assume one replica can serve **200 reads/s** at the target latency.

1. Divide peak load by capacity. **694 ÷ 200 = 3.47**.
2. Round up to **4 replicas**.
3. Use **5 replicas** to keep four serving if one fails.

> **Check.** Verify latency under concurrent load. Test uneven routing and downstream failures.

lessons.title: Vertical vs Horizontal
lessons.summary: Choose between a larger machine and more machines.

sections.visualNote: Add capacity to the existing server when the workload benefits from a larger machine.
sections.title: Scale up
sections.body:
**Scale up** by giving one machine more resources. The report service uses all **4 vCPUs** on Server A.

Give Server A **8 vCPUs**. Measure the report time again.

> **Note.** A report that uses one thread may gain little from more cores.

sections.visualNote: Both instances need to be able to process the requests sent to them.
sections.title: Scale out
sections.body:
**Scale out** by adding machines. Run **two 4-vCPU instances** and split independent reports between them.

Each instance must be able to run the reports it receives.

- Check whether the **database** limits throughput.
- Compare how long it takes to add capacity and recover from failure.

lessons.title: Load Balancing
lessons.summary: Distribute requests across healthy instances.

sections.visualNote: Server B has spare capacity, but every client connects to Server A.
sections.title: Find the overloaded server
sections.body:
The ticket site has two servers. All clients use **Server A's address**.

- **Server A:** Requests arrive faster than it can finish them. A queue builds.
- **Server B:** It has spare capacity. Clients send it no requests.
sections.bodyHtml:
The ticket site has two servers. All clients use Server A's address.

  • Server A: Requests arrive faster than it can finish them. A queue builds.
  • Server B: It has spare capacity. Clients send it no requests.

sections.note: A backend pool is the group of servers to which the load balancer can send traffic.
sections.visualNote: Publish the balancer address so backend addresses can change independently.
sections.title: Give clients one service address
sections.body:
Publish **one service address**. Clients send requests to the load balancer.

1. The balancer selects a backend.
2. It forwards the request.
3. It relays the response.

The service address stays the same when you add or replace a backend.
sections.bodyHtml:

  2. It forwards the request.
  3. It relays the response.

The service address stays the same when you add or replace a backend.

sections.note: This policy works best when servers have similar capacity and requests take a similar amount of work.
sections.visualNote: A and B take turns receiving new work when both are available.
sections.title: Take turns with round robin
sections.body:
**Round robin** takes turns across the available servers.

| Request | Server |
| --- | --- |
| First | A |
| Second | B |
| Third | A |

The cycle repeats while both servers are available.

sections.visualNote: Equal request counts can leave one server busier when request costs differ.
sections.title: Compare short and long requests
sections.body:
Opening a listing is fast. Generating a report takes longer.

Each counts as **one request**. The report holds resources for longer, so equal request counts can leave one server busier.

sections.note: Open connections approximate load. One connection can carry multiple requests, so actual server load can differ.
sections.visualNote: The example favors Server B because it has fewer open connections.
sections.title: Use the number of open connections
sections.body:
**Least connections** sends a new connection to the server with the fewest open connections.

- **Server A:** Reports still hold connections open.
- **Server B:** It has fewer open connections. It receives the next one.

sections.note: The remaining servers need enough capacity to handle the traffic after a backend fails.
sections.visualNote: Remove Server B from rotation after it fails the health check threshold.
sections.title: Route around an unhealthy server
sections.body:
Health checks help the balancer decide which servers can take new work.

1. Server B fails enough checks to reach the configured threshold.
2. The balancer stops sending it **new requests**.
3. Later, successful checks can return it to the pool.

sections.title: Check what happens when the balancer fails
sections.body:
One load balancer sits on every request path.

> **Warning.** If it fails, clients lose access even when both backend servers are healthy.

sections.visualNote: The primary serves the public address. The new standby waits in a separate failure zone.
sections.title: Prepare a standby load balancer
sections.body:
Restore the primary balancer. Give a standby the same routing rules and backend pool.

- **Primary:** Serves the public address.
- **Standby:** Checks the primary. It waits until needed.

Put the standby in a **separate failure domain** so a single host or network failure is less likely to stop both.

sections.visualNote: Measure how long the public address takes to work again after failover.
sections.title: Test the switch to standby
sections.body:
The primary fails again. The standby takes over the service address, or a routing service directs traffic to it.

New requests can reach the same backends. Measure how long the switch takes and check whether existing connections survive.

lessons.title: Stateless Services
lessons.summary: Make requests portable across service instances.

sections.visualNote: A second request can go to a different server from the first.
sections.title: Keep requests independent
sections.body:
Send a **session ID** or a **signed token** with every request.

A healthy replica can handle the request without relying on an earlier request to the same process.

Send a session ID or a signed token with every request.

sections.visualNote: Expire shared session records when the application no longer needs them.
sections.title: Move shared state
sections.body:
Some sessions need shared data that can change. Store it outside the service replicas.

- Set an **expiry** for session records.
- Give access only to the services that need it.
sections.bodyHtml:
Some sessions need shared data that can change. Store it outside the service replicas.

  • Set an expiry for session records.
  • Give access only to the services that need it.

sections.visualNote: Adding service replicas can increase load on the shared store.
sections.title: Scale and replace
sections.body:
Restart one replica during a series of requests. Send the next request to another healthy replica.

> **Watch for a bottleneck.** More service replicas can put more load on the shared store.

lessons.title: Caching
lessons.summary: Serve repeated reads faster while managing stale data.

sections.visualNote: The service reads the database on a miss and fills the cache after the read.
sections.title: Read through a cache
sections.body:
Look up **product 42** in the cache.

- **Hit:** Return the cached value.
- **Miss:** Read the database. Save a copy with an expiry.
sections.bodyHtml:
Look up product 42 in the cache.

  • Hit: Return the cached value.
  • Miss: Read the database. Save a copy with an expiry.

sections.visualNote: Set the lifetime from the amount of stale data a reader can accept.
sections.title: Set freshness rules
sections.body:
Set a **time to live (TTL)** for each cached product. Invalidate its copy after a database update commits.

> **Warning.** A concurrent reader can put an old value back in the cache. Use a version check when needed. Otherwise, choose how long users can safely see stale data.

Set a time to live (TTL) for each cached product. Invalidate its copy after a database update commits.

Warning. A concurrent reader can put an old value back in the cache. Use a version check when needed. Otherwise, choose how long users can safely see stale data.

sections.visualNote: Coalescing lets requests for the same missing key share one database query.
sections.title: Handle misses safely
sections.body:
A popular key expires. Many requests now miss at the same time.

- **Coalesce requests:** One caller reads the database. Other callers share that result.
- **Add jitter:** Vary expiry times so many keys do not expire together.

  • Average: About 4,000 events/s.
  • Peak: About 12,000 events/s at the assumed peak.

Trade-off. Best-effort events can lose counts. Durable delivery can add latency or need buffering. Use event IDs to avoid double counting on retry.

sections.title: Limit abuse
sections.body:

- Check URL schemes and destinations. Recheck as threat information changes.
- Set expiry and allow links to be disabled.
- Invalidate cached mappings when you disable a link.

> **Warning.** Define what happens if the checker is unavailable. Protect the service against server-side request forgery before it fetches a user-supplied URL.

lessons.title: Design a News Feed
lessons.summary: Design a feed by estimating fan-out, choosing when to do work, and handling freshness and access.

sections.visualNote: Authors publish posts; readers request a feed of permitted posts.
sections.title: Define the product
sections.body:
Build a **chronological feed** of posts from followed accounts.

- People can publish, read, and page through posts.
- A post can become private or be deleted.
- New posts should appear within **seconds**. A short delay is acceptable.

Ranking, ads, and media storage are out of scope. Keep the read path available. Show only posts whose access you can verify.

sections.visualNote: Reads exceed posts, but each post can produce many feed updates.
sections.title: Estimate requests and fan-out
sections.body:
Assume **10 million posts** and **100 million feed reads** per day. A day has **86,400 seconds**.

| Work | Average and 3× peak |
| --- | --- |
| Publish | **116/s** average, about 348/s peak |
| Read | **1,157/s** average, about 3,471/s peak |

With **200 followers per post**, fan-out creates **2 billion feed insertions/day**, about **23,148/s**. Measure the follower distribution before sizing workers.

sections.visualNote: Each request finds followed authors, then merges their recent posts.
sections.title: Start with a read-time merge
sections.body:
Store posts by author. Keep a record of who follows whom.

1. Fetch recent posts from followed authors.
2. Merge by creation time and a stable tie-breaker.
3. Return a page.

**Trade-off:** Publishing stays simple. Readers who follow many accounts make more work at read time. Indexes and batches help reduce lookup cost.

Assume each read looks up **200 author timelines**.

> **Note.** This counts logical lookups. A batch can serve more than one lookup in a single database call. For ordinary authors, consider doing the merge work when they publish.

sections.visualNote: A worker consumes a post event and inserts a reference into each follower's feed.
sections.title: Precompute ordinary feeds
sections.body:
1. Save the post.
2. Publish a durable event.
3. Insert a post reference into each follower's feed.

Reading a prepared list saves work at read time. The extra writes and references cost storage.

Use a **transactional outbox** or an equivalent mechanism to keep a committed post from losing its event. Make the worker safe to retry. Monitor queue age.

sections.visualNote: Ordinary posts are pushed to feeds; posts from very popular authors stay in an author timeline for read-time merge.
sections.title: Handle popular authors
sections.body:
One post from an account with **10 million followers** needs **10 million insertions** if you push it to every feed.

At **20,000 insertions/s**, that takes **500 seconds** before retries or contention. The goal is seconds.

- **Ordinary authors:** Push references into follower feeds.
- **Popular authors:** Pull recent posts at read time.

Set the threshold from measured cost and latency. Test strategy changes for missing or duplicate posts.

sections.visualNote: The service merges candidate references and returns a cursor for the next page.
sections.title: Page without losing position
sections.body:
Use a stable cursor, such as **`(created_at, post_id)`**.

1. Fetch candidates from prepared feeds and popular timelines.
2. Merge the results and remove duplicates.
3. Return the next **20 permitted posts**.

Define a snapshot boundary for new posts. Store enough merge state in the cursor to resume across sources.

sections.visualNote: Feed entries are candidate references; the service checks current visibility before returning a post.
sections.title: Enforce access and deletion
sections.body:
A feed reference can outlive an unfollow, deletion, or privacy change. Treat it as a candidate. Check **current visibility** before returning the post.

> **Warning.** If the policy service is unavailable, withhold posts you cannot verify. Fetch more candidates only up to a defined limit.

Remove old entries in the background to reduce wasted work.

lessons.title: Design a Chat System
lessons.summary: Design messaging from the delivery contract through persistence, reconnects, and scale.

sections.visualNote: A sender submits a message; the recipient may be online or offline.
sections.title: Define the contract
sections.body:
Support **one-to-one text messages**, online delivery, and catch-up after reconnect.

- Keep messages for **one year**.
- Define an order within each conversation.
- Acknowledge acceptance only after the server saves the message.

Use authorization and transport encryption. End-to-end encryption and exactly-once delivery are outside this example.

sections.visualNote: Each accepted message is stored before delivery is attempted.
sections.title: Estimate load and storage
sections.body:
Assume **10 million daily active users**. Each sends **100 messages/day**.

| Quantity | Estimate |
| --- | --- |
| Message rate | 1 billion/day ÷ 86,400 ≈ **11,574/s** |
| 3× peak | About **34,722/s** |
| Logical storage | 1 billion/day × 365 × 1 KB = **365 TB** |
| Three copies | About **1.1 PB** |

> **Assumption.** Each stored message uses 1 KB. Add indexes, backups, and storage overhead. Attachments are out of scope.

sections.visualNote: Gateways maintain client connections and forward messages to the service.
sections.title: Keep an online connection
sections.body:
Use a persistent connection such as **WebSocket**. The gateway authenticates clients and holds sender and recipient connections. Revalidate sessions when required. The chat service can scale separately.

**2 million connections ÷ 50,000 per gateway = 40 gateways** before headroom.

Allow for failures and uneven load. Test memory, file descriptors, network use, and heartbeat costs.

sections.visualNote: The server writes the message and then acknowledges the sender; recipient delivery follows separately.
sections.title: Persist before acknowledging
sections.body:
The client sends a **message ID**, **conversation ID**, and **body**.

1. Check conversation membership.
2. Assign a sequence and persist the message.
3. Acknowledge acceptance after the durable write.

Use a unique key for the sender and client message ID. A retry with the same payload returns the prior result and sequence. Define how long to keep the key.

> **Note.** Acceptance means the server saved the message. The recipient may still be offline.

sections.visualNote: A worker consumes a stored delivery event and uses the directory to find the recipient gateway.
sections.title: Route to online recipients
sections.body:
1. Save the message and its **outbox record** in one transaction.
2. A relay publishes an event to the delivery queue.
3. A worker looks up the recipient's current gateway.
4. The gateway pushes the message.

> **Warning.** A connection can disappear between lookup and send. Retry when useful. Clients can recover from durable history. Consumers must handle repeated events after a relay failure.

sections.visualNote: The client requests messages after its last confirmed sequence and removes duplicates by message ID.
sections.title: Recover after reconnect
sections.body:
On reconnect, the client sends the last **contiguous sequence** it saved. The service returns later messages in pages.

- Deduplicate by **message ID**.
- Advance the cursor only after saving a contiguous range.
- Report a gap if retention removed messages in that range.

A lost acknowledgment can cause delivery of the same message again.

sections.visualNote: A conversation's writes receive a stable order before clients consume them.
sections.title: Preserve conversation order
sections.body:
Two users can send at the same time. Assign increasing sequences **per conversation**. Use one owner or an atomic storage operation.

Order messages by that sequence. Coordinate sequence assignment with the write so failures leave a clear result.

> **Note.** A busy group can overload its own partition. Measure that load before changing how the system assigns ownership.

sections.title: Secure and operate the service
sections.body:
- Encrypt traffic in transit and protect stored data.
- Authorize every send and history request.
- Limit abusive traffic and expire messages on schedule.

> **Warning.** A removed member must stop receiving new messages, even on an existing connection.

Monitor write latency, queue age, delivery lag, connection churn, and reconnect errors. Test both gateway and store outages.
